assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Fluorescent stains
items.clue: Dyes that absorb light of one wavelength and emit light of a longer wavelength.

items.label: Resolution
items.clue: The smallest distance between two points at which they can still be seen as separate.

items.label: Scale bar
items.clue: A line drawn on a micrograph or drawing that represents a stated actual length in the specimen, for example 10 µm.

items.label: Immunofluorescence
items.clue: A light microscopy technique in which antibodies that bind specifically to one protein are linked to a fluorescent marker.

questions.stem: In a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of ×2000, a red blood cell measures 15 mm across. What is the actual width of the cell?

options.text: 7.5 µm

questions.explanation: Actual size = size of image ÷ magnification = 15 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.0075 mm, which is 7.5 µm (1 mm = 1000 µm), the typical diameter of a red blood cell.

questions.stem: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across. They cannot be seen with a light microscope but are clearly visible in electron micrographs. What is the reason?

options.text: The electron microscope magnifies many more times, so much smaller objects become visible.
Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so the resolution is much higher.
Heavy-metal stains used for electron microscopy make small structures much sharper.
Electron microscopes use fluorescent stains that make ribosomes glow in the dark.

questions.stem: With the ×40 objective lens in place, 40 divisions of an eyepiece graticule line up exactly with 100 µm on a stage micrometer. Using the same objective, a cell spans 44 graticule divisions. What is the actual length of the cell in millimetres?

options.text: 1.1 mm

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of cryogenic electron microscopy over conventional electron microscopy?

options.text: Rapid freezing keeps unfixed, unstained molecules near their natural state, so structures are resolved in near-atomic detail.
Heavy-metal stains bind more firmly at very low temperature, so the contrast between structures in the specimen is much greater.
Freezing makes the cell brittle, so it can be fractured to reveal the interior of its membranes in section.
The very low temperature prevents the electron beam from killing the cells, so living cells can be observed in action.

questions.stem: A student makes a drawing of a cell at a magnification of ×1250 and wants to add a scale bar representing 10 µm. How long should the scale bar be drawn?

options.text: 125 mm
10 mm

questions.explanation: The drawn length of a scale bar is the actual length it represents multiplied by the magnification: 10 µm × 1250 = 12 500 µm = 12.5 mm.

questions.stem: A student focuses a stained temporary mount at low power, then rotates the high-power objective lens into place. The image is now slightly blurred. What should the student do?

options.text: Turn only the fine adjustment until the image is sharp.
Turn the coarse adjustment, since it changes the focus most quickly.
Add more stain to the mount so the structures show up clearly.
Switch to an even higher-power objective lens to enlarge the details.

questions.explanation: At high power the objective is close to the slide and the depth of focus is very small, so the fine adjustment is the only focusing control used; it moves the lens by tiny amounts to sharpen the image without risk to the slide or lens.

questions.stem: On pre-biotic Earth, ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface far more than it does today. What is the reason for this?

options.text: There was no free oxygen, so no ozone could form to absorb the radiation.
The methane and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere had destroyed the ozone layer.
Free oxygen was used up oxidizing methane before it could form ozone.
The high temperatures broke down ozone as fast as it was produced.

questions.explanation: Ozone (O₃) is made from oxygen (O₂) by ultraviolet light in the upper atmosphere. Pre-biotic Earth lacked free oxygen and therefore lacked ozone, so ultraviolet radiation was not absorbed and reached the surface.

questions.stem: Which statement gives a reason that viruses are considered to be non-living?

options.text: They are cells that are too small to hold the organelles needed for metabolism.
They are not whole organisms, and only complete organisms are living.
They carry out no metabolism and can only replicate using a host cell.
They have genes and can evolve, but they do not have a nucleus.

questions.explanation: A virus has no enzymes for metabolism and cannot grow, respond or maintain itself. New virus particles are made by the host cell's machinery, so a virus is not self-sustaining, which is why it is considered non-living.

questions.stem: Which set of processes is regarded as the necessary requirements for the evolution of the first cells?

options.text: Catalysis, self-replication of molecules, self-assembly and the emergence of compartmentalization
A single improbable chance event assembling a complete cell with all of its parts at once
Formation of DNA, then transcription and translation, before any membrane had formed
Continuing spontaneous generation of whole cells from non-living matter in pond water

questions.stem: In the Miller–Urey experiment, a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour was exposed to electrical sparks for a week. Which conclusion is supported by the products that were found?

options.text: Living cells can form from inorganic molecules given an energy source and enough time.
The twenty amino acids used in proteins are the only products that such conditions make.
Amino acids and other carbon compounds can form abiotically under such conditions.
Carbon compounds can form only where living organisms are already present.

questions.stem: Why was the formation of membrane-bound compartments a necessary step in the origin of cells?

options.text: It shielded the enclosed molecules from the ultraviolet light that reached the surface.
It allowed the chemistry inside the compartment to become different from that of the outside.
It provided a solid droplet of lipid inside which the first chemical reactions could occur.
It allowed a complete cell to assemble in a single step from the molecules dissolved in the water.

questions.stem: Why is RNA, rather than DNA, presumed to have been the first genetic material?

options.text: RNA formed as single-stranded copies made from the very first DNA molecules to exist.
RNA is simpler than DNA, so it is more stable and survived for longer in the early oceans.
RNA can be replicated and is catalytic, so it could serve as both genes and enzymes.
RNA was needed to code for the proteins that acted as the very first enzymes.
